credit_headline.narrative: Bank credit reached ₹215.2L Cr in May 2026, the highest level on record, with year-on-year growth at 17.7% — the fastest rate in this nine-period window. The system added ₹31.2L Cr in FY26, the largest annual deployment tracked here, and growth re-accelerated in May after a brief April pause. All four main sectors — agriculture, industry, services, retail — have posted positive growth in every period since January 2025, with breadth holding at 4 out of 4. Non-food credit drives the expansion, now at ₹213.8L Cr and growing 17.4% year-on-year, while food credit surged to ₹1.37L Cr on 94.1% growth, reflecting active procurement financing.

sibc-pl-gold-share.direction: Share climbed from 7.02% in Apr 2026 to 7.33% in May 2026, continuing the surge from 3.0% in Jan 2025.
chain: Gold loans now hold 7.33% of personal loans, up 0.31 points from last period and more than double the 3.0% share in Jan 2025.

Gold is displacing other categories in a growing pool — it is capturing incremental flows faster than any other segment.
sibc-pl-gold-share.inference: Gold lending has become a structural pillar of retail credit. The 7.33% share is small in absolute terms, but the trajectory is steep — gold is the fastest-growing pocket in personal loans and is reshaping the mix.

Despite the deceleration, the 105.5% pace still far outstrips all other personal loan categories — gold is doubling year-on-year while housing grows at 10.9% and other PL at 12.5%.
sibc-pl-gold-yoy.inference: Gold lending remains the fastest-growing personal loan category by a wide margin, but the explosive phase is cooling. The 15.7-point deceleration is the first sharp step-down after six months of plateau — watch for whether this is a one-period correction or the start of a sustained moderation.

sibc-infra-sub-yoy-scan.title: Ports surged 82.8% YoY — Railways collapsed -37.6%
sibc-infra-sub-yoy-scan.observation: Ports grew 82.8% year-on-year, Power 23.8%, and Other Infrastructure 1.5%. Railways (other than Indian Railways) contracted -37.6%, Airports -14.5%, and Telecommunications -7.0%.
sibc-infra-sub-yoy-scan.direction: Ports accelerated from 74.0% to 82.8% and remains strengthening. Power shifted from active to strengthening at 23.8%, up from 21.5%. Roads flipped from active to declining at -0.7%. The spread is 120.4 percentage points — the widest in this window.
chain: Ports grew 82.8% YoY, the fastest in Infrastructure and up from 74.0% last period.
Power shifted to strengthening at 23.8%, while Roads turned negative at -0.7% and Railways deepened to -37.6%.
The 120.4-point spread confirms extreme polarisation: trade and energy infrastructure are surging while transport segments contract.

Roads has turned negative for the first time in this window, and Railways remains in sharp contraction at -37.6% — project delays or lender exits are likely. The 120.4-point spread is the widest on record, confirming Infrastructure credit is bifurcating into winners (Ports, Power) and losers (transport).

sibc-large-corporate-share.title: Large corporates at 67.3% share — down 3.8pp in 15 months
sibc-large-corporate-share.observation: Large corporates account for 67.3% of industry credit in May 2026, up 0.11pp from the prior period.
sibc-large-corporate-share.direction: Share compressed from 71.0% in Jan 2025 to 66.8% in Jan 2026, then stabilised at 67.1% → 67.2% → 67.2% → 67.3% over the last four periods — a net loss of 3.7 percentage points since Jan 2025.
chain: Large corporates hold 67.3% of industry credit, up 0.11pp from last period but down 3.7pp from 71.0% in Jan 2025.
The share has plateaued at 67.1%–67.3% for four consecutive periods after a sharp 4.2pp drop from Jan 2025 to Jan 2026.
The structural loss confirms incremental credit is flowing disproportionately to MSME borrowers, not large corporates.
sibc-large-corporate-share.inference: Large corporates have lost 3.7 percentage points of industry credit in 15 months and are now holding steady at 67.3%. The four-period plateau signals the share erosion has paused, but the segment is no longer capturing the bulk of incremental credit — that flow is going to Micro & Small borrowers.

sibc-large-corporate-yoy.title: Large corporates hit 14.4% YoY — fastest in this window
sibc-large-corporate-yoy.observation: Large corporate credit grew 14.4% YoY in May 2026, the strongest reading in this nine-period window.
sibc-large-corporate-yoy.direction: Growth accelerated from 10.0% last period to 14.4%, extending a recovery that began at 5.5% in Jan 2026. The trajectory is 6.8% → 5.6% → 6.9% → 7.5% → 5.5% → 7.8% → 9.1% → 10.0% → 14.4%.
chain: Large corporate credit grew 14.4% YoY, up from 10.0% last period and the fastest in this nine-period window.
The segment has re-accelerated from a low of 5.5% in Jan 2026, gaining 8.9 percentage points in four periods.
Despite the acceleration, large corporates are losing share because MSME segments are growing faster — Micro & Small at 26.2%, Medium at 21.2%.
sibc-large-corporate-yoy.inference: Large corporates are re-accelerating and have hit the fastest growth rate in this window at 14.4%. The 8.9-point gain from Jan 2026 is a sharp recovery. However, the segment is still losing share because MSME growth remains structurally higher — the 14.4% pace is healthy but insufficient to defend market position.

sibc-msme-medium-share.title: Medium enterprises at 9.7% share — flat for five periods
sibc-msme-medium-share.observation: Medium enterprises account for 9.7% of industry credit in May 2026, down 0.05pp from the prior period.
sibc-msme-medium-share.direction: Share rose from 8.9% in Jan 2025 to 9.7% by Jan 2026 and has held at 9.7% for five consecutive periods — a net gain of 0.8 percentage points since Jan 2025.
chain: Medium enterprises hold 9.7% of industry credit, unchanged for five straight periods after rising from 8.9% in Jan 2025.
The five-period plateau signals the segment is growing in line with the broader industry pool, not outpacing it.
The 0.8pp gain from Jan 2025 to Jan 2026 was a structural shift, but the segment has since stabilised.
sibc-msme-medium-share.inference: Medium enterprises have carved out a 9.7% share and are holding it. The five-period plateau confirms the segment is growing in line with industry credit, not capturing outsized incremental flow. The 0.8pp gain from Jan 2025 to Jan 2026 was a one-time structural shift, now complete.

sibc-msme-medium-yoy.title: Medium enterprises at 21.2% YoY — re-accelerating
sibc-msme-medium-yoy.observation: Medium enterprise credit grew 21.2% YoY in May 2026, up 1.29pp from the prior period.
sibc-msme-medium-yoy.direction: Growth re-accelerated from 19.9% last period to 21.2%, after decelerating from a peak of 22.3% in Jan 2026. The trajectory is 18.4% → 18.0% → 18.5% → 20.4% → 22.3% → 21.0% → 21.8% → 19.9% → 21.2%.
chain: Medium enterprise credit grew 21.2% YoY, up from 19.9% last period and re-accelerating after a two-period deceleration.
The segment peaked at 22.3% in Jan 2026, dipped to 19.9% in Apr 2026, and has now recovered to 21.2%.
The 21.2% pace is far ahead of large corporates at 14.4% but below Micro & Small at 26.2%.
sibc-msme-medium-yoy.inference: Medium enterprises are re-accelerating after a brief deceleration. The 21.2% pace is healthy and far ahead of large corporates, but the segment is not the fastest-growing — Micro & Small at 26.2% is outpacing it. The re-acceleration confirms Medium remains a strong outperformer, but momentum is concentrating in smaller borrowers.

sibc-msme-micro-small-fy-acceleration.title: Micro & Small grew 32.7% in FY26 vs 8.9% in FY25 — 23.8pp step-up
sibc-msme-micro-small-fy-acceleration.observation: Micro & Small credit grew 8.9% in the year ending Mar 2025 and 32.7% in the year ending Mar 2026, a 23.8 percentage point acceleration.
sibc-msme-micro-small-fy-acceleration.direction: Full-year growth jumped from 8.9% in FY25 to 32.7% in FY26 — the sharpest year-over-year step-up in this dataset.
chain: Micro & Small credit grew 8.9% in FY25 and 32.7% in FY26, a 23.8 percentage point acceleration.
The 23.8pp step-up is the largest full-year acceleration in this dataset, confirming a structural inflection.
Lenders with exposure to Micro & Small are riding the fastest-growing segment in industry credit.
sibc-msme-micro-small-fy-acceleration.inference: This is the defining inflection in industry credit. Micro & Small lending has entered a new growth regime, and the 23.8pp step-up from FY25 to FY26 is unprecedented in this dataset. Banks and NBFCs scaling this segment are capturing outsized share of incremental credit.

sibc-msme-micro-small-share.title: Micro & Small at 23.1% share — up 3.1pp in 14 months
sibc-msme-micro-small-share.observation: Micro & Small enterprises account for 23.1% of industry credit in May 2026, down 0.06pp from the prior period.
sibc-msme-micro-small-share.direction: Share surged from 20.0% in Mar 2025 to 23.5% in Jan 2026, then eased to 23.1% → 23.2% → 23.1% → 23.1% → 23.1% over the last five periods — a net gain of 3.1 percentage points since Mar 2025.
chain: Micro & Small borrowers hold 23.1% of industry credit, down 0.06pp from last period but up 3.1pp from 20.0% in Mar 2025.
The share peaked at 23.5% in Jan 2026 and has since stabilised at 23.1%–23.2% for five consecutive periods.
The 3.1pp gain in 14 months is a structural reallocation, coming at the expense of large corporates who lost 3.7pp over the same window.
sibc-msme-micro-small-share.inference: Micro & Small borrowers are capturing share at the expense of large corporates. The 3.1pp gain in 14 months is a structural reallocation, not noise. The five-period plateau at 23.1% signals the segment is now growing in line with the broader pool, having completed a sharp share grab from Mar 2025 to Jan 2026.

sibc-msme-micro-small-yoy.title: Micro & Small at 26.2% YoY — decelerating but still fastest
sibc-msme-micro-small-yoy.observation: Micro & Small credit grew 26.2% YoY in May 2026, down 3.91pp from the prior period.
sibc-msme-micro-small-yoy.direction: Growth decelerated from 30.1% last period to 26.2%, after peaking at 32.7% in Mar 2026. The trajectory is 9.6% → 9.6% → 8.9% → 31.0% → 31.2% → 30.4% → 32.7% → 30.1% → 26.2%.
chain: Micro & Small credit grew 26.2% YoY, down from 30.1% last period and the slowest since the segment exploded from 8.9% in Mar 2025.
The segment peaked at 32.7% in Mar 2026 and has now decelerated for two consecutive periods, losing 6.5 percentage points.
Despite the deceleration, 26.2% is still the fastest growth rate in industry credit — ahead of Medium at 21.2% and Large at 14.4%.
sibc-msme-micro-small-yoy.inference: Micro & Small is decelerating but remains the hottest segment in industry credit. The 6.5-point drop from the Mar 2026 peak is notable, but the 26.2% pace is still far ahead of all other segments. The deceleration is worth watching — if growth drops below 20%, the segment risks losing its share-gaining momentum.

sibc-msme-size-yoy-spread.title: MSME-Large spread at 11.8pp — narrowest since Mar 2025
sibc-msme-size-yoy-spread.observation: MSME credit is growing 11.8 percentage points faster than large corporate credit in May 2026.
sibc-msme-size-yoy-spread.direction: The spread narrowed from 20.1pp last period to 11.8pp, the smallest gap since 2.1pp in Mar 2025. The trajectory is 2.8pp → 4.0pp → 2.1pp → 23.5pp → 25.7pp → 22.6pp → 23.5pp → 20.1pp → 11.8pp.
chain: The MSME-Large growth spread is 11.8 percentage points, down from 20.1pp last period and the narrowest since Mar 2025.
The spread peaked at 25.7pp in Jan 2026 and has now narrowed for three consecutive periods, losing 13.9 points.
The narrowing is driven by large corporates re-accelerating to 14.4% while Micro & Small decelerated to 26.2%.
sibc-msme-size-yoy-spread.inference: The growth divergence between MSME and large corporates is narrowing sharply. Large corporates are re-accelerating and closing the gap, but MSME segments are still growing nearly twice as fast. The 11.8pp spread is the narrowest since the MSME surge began, signaling large corporates are regaining momentum — but incremental credit is still flowing disproportionately to smaller borrowers.

sibc-textiles-sub-share-scan.title: Other Textiles at 45.3% share — Cotton slipping to 35.6%
sibc-textiles-sub-share-scan.observation: Within Textiles, Other Textiles accounts for 45.3% of credit, Cotton Textiles 35.6%, Man-Made 17.3%, and Jute 1.7%.
sibc-textiles-sub-share-scan.direction: Other Textiles shifted from active to strengthening and now holds 45.3% share. Cotton Textiles shifted from active to weakening at 35.6%. The four sub-segments span a 43.6 percentage point range, with Other and Cotton together holding 80.9% of the pool.
chain: Other Textiles holds 45.3% of Textiles credit and shifted to strengthening status, while Cotton Textiles slipped to 35.6% and shifted to weakening.
Other and Cotton together account for 80.9% of the pool, down from 81.2% last period.
The status shifts confirm Other is gaining share at Cotton's expense.
sibc-textiles-sub-share-scan.inference: Textiles credit is concentrating in Other, which shifted to strengthening at 45.3% share, while Cotton shifted to weakening at 35.6%. The two largest segments together hold 80.9% of the pool, and the status shifts confirm a structural reallocation from Cotton to Other. Man-Made and Jute remain too small to matter.

sibc-textiles-sub-yoy-scan.title: Jute surged 20.2% YoY — Cotton slowest at 3.2%
sibc-textiles-sub-yoy-scan.observation: Within Textiles, Jute credit grew 20.2% YoY, Other Textiles 17.1%, Man-Made 8.1%, and Cotton Textiles 3.2%.
sibc-textiles-sub-yoy-scan.direction: Other Textiles shifted from active to strengthening at 17.1%, up from 13.3% last period. Man-Made shifted from active to strengthening at 8.1%, up from 2.7%. Cotton shifted from strengthening to active at 3.2%, down from 4.8%. The spread across the four segments is 17.0 percentage points.
chain: Jute grew 20.2% YoY, the fastest in Textiles, while Cotton slowed to 3.2%, the weakest reading.
Other Textiles re-accelerated to 17.1% and shifted to strengthening, while Man-Made jumped to 8.1% and also shifted to strengthening.
Cotton decelerated to 3.2% and shifted from strengthening to active, confirming it is the laggard.
sibc-textiles-sub-yoy-scan.inference: Textiles credit is in a broad-based recovery, but momentum is concentrating in Jute and Other. Other Textiles re-accelerated to 17.1% and shifted to strengthening, while Man-Made jumped to 8.1% and also shifted to strengthening. Cotton is the weakest link at 3.2%, down from 4.8% last period and now in active status — the largest segment by share is the slowest by growth.
